# The Collector of Last Sounds

I have spent forty years recording things as they end.

It began by accident. My father owned a reel-to-reel machine, heavy as a sleeping dog, and one summer evening he set it on the porch rail to capture the crickets. He never played the tape back. After he died, I found it in a box labeled MISC., and when I finally threaded it through a player—decades later—the crickets came up out of the silence so suddenly that I looked around the room as though they'd followed me indoors. Then I understood what I was hearing: not crickets, but that particular summer, that particular porch, the particular heat rising off the driveway in waves you couldn't see but could almost hear, a shimmer beneath the insect noise. My father coughed once, off-microphone, and shifted the machine, and the world tilted slightly in the speakers. He had been dead eleven years. The porch had been torn down. The crickets, wherever they were, were singing different songs now.

That was the night I became a collector of last sounds.

People assume I hunt the dramatic farewells—the last wolf in a valley, a dying language's final speaker. I've recorded those, and they matter. But the endings that undo me are smaller. The ice cream truck in our town changed its song in 1994 from "Turkey in the Straw" to a digital chime, and no one thought to preserve the old bell-and-comb mechanism grinding out its warped notes down Maple Street. The sound of a rotary phone dialed by someone who knows the number by heart—that muscle-memory clatter and whir, quicker than any young person manages, because the fingers remember even when the mind stumbles. The specific squeak of gym sneakers on waxed hardwood before a tip-off, the hush, the referee's whistle with its pea rattling inside like a tiny heart.

I drove three hundred miles once to record the Kettle Falls ferry horn before the new bridge silenced it forever. Stood on the dock at dawn with my parabolic microphone aimed into the fog. What I hadn't planned for was the gulls. They'd nested in the horn's housing, and when the horn sounded, they lifted off all at once—a white detonation of wings against gray water—and their cries braided through the horn's low note until I couldn't tell alarm from announcement. The bridge engineers hadn't considered the gulls. Honestly, neither had I. That recording exists now, and every time I play it I hear not just a horn dying but a whole small civilization dispersing into the air, scattering over water that would forget them by noon.

Here is what I have learned: nothing ends once. A sound dies the way a star does, its light arriving long after the source goes dark. My mother's voice survives on an answering-machine cassette—*We can't come to the phone right now*—and each playback wears the oxide a little thinner, drops a little more signal into noise. I have played it exactly twice in fifteen years. There are people who digitize such things, transfer everything to pristine files, and I understand them, but I can't bring myself to do it. As long as her voice lives on that degrading ribbon, it is still, technically, dying rather than dead—and there is a difference, the way a candle guttering is different from a dark room.

Or maybe that's superstition. Maybe it's just grief wearing headphones.

Last spring I attempted to record what may be the final performance of a nightingale population on the southern coast. I waited four nights in a salt marsh with equipment worth more than my car. On the fifth night, one sang: that impossible spill of notes, improvisation folded over improvisation, a bird inventing itself again and again out of pure excess. I got eleven minutes. In those eleven minutes there is wind, a distant truck, my own breath caught by the microphone like an intruder. Some archivists would call that contamination. I call it proof of attendance.

A young colleague asked me recently why any of it matters—who will listen to these files in a hundred years, and what will ferries and phone dials and birds mean to them? I told her about my father's crickets. How I've played that tape perhaps fifty times, and how each time, for ninety seconds, I am nine years old on that porch, watching fireflies stitch themselves into the dark while a man I loved fiddles with dials beside me. The recording doesn't preserve the past. It preserves *access* to it. That's different, and the difference is everything.

She nodded politely, the way the young do when an old man gets mystical about tape hiss.

But consider this: right now, somewhere near you, a sound is sounding for the last time. The particular rattle of a radiator in a house about to be demolished. A grandmother's laugh in a kitchen that will be renovated by June. The fourth note of a carillon that sits slightly flat because the bellcaster in 1911 misjudged the pour—a mistake no one will ever cast again. You cannot save them all. I've stopped pretending otherwise. The archive is not salvation. It is witness.

So tonight I did what I sometimes do. I threaded my father's tape, let the crickets rise, let the porch tilt, let him cough off-microphone and adjust the machine. Ninety seconds of a vanished summer. Then I stopped the tape mid-song, the way you leave a door ajar, and sat in the dark listening to the present tense—the refrigerator humming, the traffic arriving like surf, my own breathing going unrecorded, unrecordable, already ending, already enough.
